Compared all three questions, six response parts and data displays against the source image and teaching 82. Pre/post frequencies [4,7,9,5,4,1] and [1,2,6,10,7,4] each total 30, with means 61/30 and 92/30 and modes 2 and 3; improvement is supported for the group. Women’s ages cluster in the 50s/60s with a left tail, men’s in the 40s with a right tail. Retirement frequencies total 2000 thousand; 35/2000=7/400=0.0175=1.75%. The 61–65 peak and longer lower tail support negative skew. Follow the source’s explicit fraction method; page 82 does not teach relative frequency, so later teaching mapping must reference 86 or flag missing earlier context.
Calculate a specified class frequency as a fraction of the total, coordinating the table’s thousands unit, then read the distribution’s peak and longer tail. These are routine linked operations; the historical Band5 label does not determine this rating.

Compared all fourteen source prompts and model critiques against teaching 89. Checked each intended target population and coverage issue. Replaced categorical claims about group preferences with likely over- or underrepresentation; conditional populations are explicit for b,h,k,l,m,n. Part g specifies teenage interviewees. Email responses, subscriber feedback and radio voting can also involve volunteer bias. The Year 7 answer explains omitted year groups rather than presuming ignorance. Multiple supported contextual explanations remain acceptable.
Explain how a sampling frame or voluntary response may differ from its target population across varied contexts. The hardest cases require a conditional target-population assumption and a likely direction of overrepresentation; fourteen repetitions do not create a higher band.

Compared both questions, the cartoon’s chart, legend, 500-response quotation and aircraft damage diagram against teaching 89. Percentages sum to 100%; 500×0.998=499 and 500×0.002=1, so people who dislike surveys are underrepresented rather than universally excluded. Returning aircraft omit failures; hits in unmarked areas may prevent return, but the diagram cannot prove every such hit fatal. Preserve actual artwork, attribution and meaningful red damage marks. All explanations independently checked.
Explain why willingness to respond selects a group whose views cannot justify the population claim. Connect the cartoon’s conclusion to the response mechanism; recognising that some dissenters still respond avoids an absolute-exclusion misconception.
